channel.title: Behavioural Science Daily Brief
channel.description: A daily reading of new working papers, peer-reviewed articles and policy work in behavioural science, psychology and behavioural economics, prepared for a first-year undergraduate on the LSE BSc Psychological and Behavioural Science. Each episode gives the finding, the method, the sample and the limitations, with a concept of the day and a note on research methods.

item.title: Saturday 17 October 2026
item.description: Most voters decide on one feature and stop, and why oxytocin is not a prosocial hormone. Also a within-family study of attention deficit traits, relational mobility and shared reality, smartphones displacing study time, sleep loss ending a lift early, and a flagged paper on ageing and inhibition.

item.title: Friday 16 October 2026
item.description: A quota whose losers are counted as well as its winners, and why a robust effect makes a poor measure. Also two brain signatures of task switching, empathy as a joint construction, a serial mediation model read as a warning, zebra finches and pitch, and a commentary without an abstract.

item.title: Thursday 15 October 2026
item.description: Automatic imitation in twenty-two countries, and why the average household that policy is written for does not exist. Also designed memorability, couples after a stroke, AI-drafted petitions, safe reinforcement learning, and two essays from the department's own blog.

item.title: Wednesday 14 October 2026
item.description: Why the paracetamol signal fades as the evidence improves, and the perspective gap that makes a silence hurt. Also genotype-guided prescribing, children's risk preferences, autism diagnosed early and late, and an LSE team reading a hundred and fifty thousand complaint responses.

item.title: Tuesday 13 October 2026
item.description: Why language models are poor stand-ins for human economic preferences, and what a life-satisfaction question measures. Also polygenic indices and voting, musicians and the ventriloquism illusion, hippocampal replay, statistical power, and patience at university.

item.title: Monday 12 October 2026
item.description: What a randomised trial can and cannot establish about systemic discrimination, plus attention and allergic reactions. Also boredom and aggression, antidepressants in pregnancy, techno-optimistic scientists, long-term single adults, and an LSE project on curiosity.

item.title: Sunday 11 October 2026
item.description: Belief in demons tracks structural explanations of poverty while belief in a supportive God tracks the opposite; incentivised patience and risk aversion predict which degree young Danes apply for; able women are read as hostile by their colleagues and able men are not. The concept of the day is attribution, dispositional against situational, from the psychological science course.

item.title: Saturday 10 October 2026
item.description: A thin day, declared as such. Singapore recruiters say they hire on merit and then penalise parents; the mental load predicts relationship satisfaction better than the washing-up does; women choose workplaces by who already works there. The concept of the day is stated preference against revealed preference, from the behavioural science course.

item.title: Friday 9 October 2026
item.description: Seven items, all published yesterday. Microdelays of a second or two measurably damage online learning; a Swedish twin study takes apart the screen-time and depression association; eye contact gates word learning in nine-month-olds. The concept of the day is the co-twin comparison, from the statistics and methods course.

item.title: Thursday 8 October 2026
item.description: Relative coding is the concept of the day: why the brain stores relations rather than absolute values. Also imagined melodies read off the cortex as intervals, a lottery windfall that changes men's marriages and women's divorces, conservatives who think rigidly without following their party, opposite reward circuitry in ADHD and autism, and a methods watch on an effect that loses most of itself to one control variable.

item.title: Wednesday 7 October 2026
item.description: Normative versus informational influence is the concept of the day, worked through a study in which people restated their politics to match a room full of chatbots. Also a parenting programme that looked like a failure for a decade until the schools closed, negativity bias in thirty-five years of newspaper text, a prediction market where position limits left free money on the screen, and a methods watch on why a properly randomised trial can still overstate its effect.

item.title: Tuesday 6 October 2026
item.description: Algorithm-assisted vaccination nudges and a transparency null; SNAP drink restrictions and mental accounting; daughters and managerial hiring as a natural experiment; contract ratios in Irish hospitals; two decades of panel data against the gender-equality paradox; crime footage and policy thresholds. Concept of the day: quasi-random variation.
